meta.descriptionEn: November 1929. A Ford Trimotor named Floyd Bennett sits on the ice of Antarctica, loaded with fuel and facing the high Antarctic Plateau between it and the South Pole. Four men, Richard Byrd, Bernt Balchen, Harold June and Ashley McKinley, must climb higher than the plane wants to go. What would they give up to make it? In this documentary we follow Byrd's first Antarctic expedition from the base at Little America to the first flight to the South Pole and back, look at the men who made it happen, and ask how much of the story we can trust. Watch to the end to see what the flight changed for Byrd, for aviation and for polar exploration.
meta.descriptionUr: Nawambar 1929 mein Antarctica ki barf par ek Ford Trimotor jahaz khara tha, jis ke samne unchi Antarctic Plateau thi. Is documentary mein hum Little America ke base se us pehli parwaz tak ka safar dekhenge, un logon ko jaanenge jinhon ne yeh mumkin banaya, aur samjhenge ke is parwaz ke baad kya badla. articleEn: On 28 November 1929, a Ford Trimotor named the Floyd Bennett was struggling to gain height over Antarctica. Below lay a plain of ice, and ahead rose the Antarctic Plateau. The plane had trouble reaching a suitable altitude, so the crew made a hard decision: the empty gas tanks and the emergency supplies were thrown out of the aircraft.

The flight began at the Little America base camp. Reaching the South Pole and returning took 18 hours and 41 minutes in total. Four men were aboard: Richard Byrd, Bernt Balchen, Harold June and Ashley McKinley. They were flying over territory where the chance of help was very small. According to the Navy Cross citation, the plane had to pass over ranges and plateaus nine to ten thousand feet high.

So why were the supplies thrown out? And what would have happened to the crew if the plane had been forced down? There is another question too. Byrd's 1926 North Pole flight is still debated today, so can this story be trusted? In this article we look at the sources to see who Byrd was, what his crew was like, and what happened on 29 November. This was not just a flight. It is a story of courage, calculation and sacrifice. Let us begin at the start.

articleEn: First, a step back. Richard Evelyn Byrd Jr. was born on 25 October 1888 in Winchester, Virginia. His brother Harry F. Byrd later became governor of Virginia and a U.S. Senator, and the family was counted among Virginia's old, prominent families. Byrd studied for two years at the Virginia Military Institute, then went to the University of Virginia. On 28 May 1908 he finally became a midshipman at the United States Naval Academy, and on 8 June 1912 he became an ensign. In the Caribbean he rescued a sailor who had fallen into the sea, and he later received the Silver Lifesaving Medal for it.

His next posting was the gunboat USS Dolphin, which was also the Secretary of the Navy's yacht. There he came into contact with senior officers, including Franklin Roosevelt. Then he suffered an ankle injury aboard the presidential yacht USS Mayflower. On 15 March 1916 he was retired on medical grounds, and he was deeply disappointed. But the story did not end there. When America entered the First World War in 1917, Byrd was called back to active duty. He became naval aviator number 608 at the naval aviation school in Pensacola in June 1918, and then took command of naval air forces at Halifax, Nova Scotia.

In 1919 the Navy prepared the first aerial transatlantic crossing. Byrd could not join the crew himself, because a tour of duty in Newfoundland counted as overseas service. But his skill in aerial navigation proved useful, and he was given the job of planning the mission's flight path. Three flying boats set out, but only the NC-4 completed the journey, on 18 May 1919, becoming the first transatlantic flight.

In 1921 Byrd offered himself for a solo nonstop crossing of the Atlantic, six years before Lindbergh's flight. But acting Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt Jr. thought the risk outweighed the benefit, so Byrd's wish went unfulfilled. He was then assigned to the airship ZR-2, but on 24 August 1921 he missed the train. The airship broke apart in the air, and 44 of the 49 people aboard died. Byrd lost many friends in the accident. It affected him deeply, and safety became his first priority in every later expedition.

In 1925 Byrd led the aviation unit on Donald MacMillan's Greenland expedition. That mission did not reach the pole, but the aircraft played a successful part. It was on this expedition that he met Floyd Bennett and the Norwegian pilot Bernt Balchen. These two names would become very important in Byrd's story.

articleEn: On 9 May 1926, Byrd and Navy pilot Floyd Bennett flew toward the North Pole in the Fokker tri-motor Josephine Ford, named after Edsel Ford's daughter. The flight began at Spitsbergen and returned there, taking 15 hours and 57 minutes in all. The two men claimed to have reached the North Pole. On his return Byrd became a national hero, with a parade in New York. On 21 December 1926 Congress, through a special act, gave Byrd the rank of commander, and both men received the Medal of Honor.

Doubts, however, were raised from 1926 onward. In 1958 Bernt Balchen questioned Byrd's claim on the basis of the aircraft's speed. According to Balchen, Bennett later admitted that they had not reached the pole. But Bennett's interviews and article give the same account as Byrd's. In 1996 the diary of Byrd's flight came to light. It contained erased but legible sextant readings that differed from the later official report. In the diary the observed height of the sun was 19 degrees 25 minutes 30 seconds, while the typed report gave 18 degrees 18 minutes 18 seconds for the same moment.

According to Dennis Rawlins, Byrd flew about 80 percent of the distance and turned back because of an oil leak. He believes the official report was changed afterward. One defender suggests that a tailwind may have increased the speed. Rawlins says the precision of the sextant data in the typed report was not possible with 1926 Navy sextants. If Byrd and Bennett did not reach the pole, the first flight over the pole was that of the airship Norge on 12 May 1926. Norge flew nonstop from Spitsbergen to Alaska, and its crew included Roald Amundsen and Umberto Nobile.

In 1927 Byrd was among several pilots who tried to win the Orteig Prize, offered for the first nonstop flight between America and France. In a practice takeoff Byrd's plane, the America, crashed and Bennett was injured. During the repairs, on 21 May 1927, Charles Lindbergh won the prize. Balchen replaced Bennett as chief pilot.

On 29 June 1927, Byrd, Balchen, Bert Acosta and George Noville left Roosevelt Field in the America. Because of clouds over France, landing in Paris was not possible. On 1 July 1927 the plane crash-landed near the shore at Ver-sur-Mer in Normandy, and everyone survived. The crew was welcomed as heroes in France, and on 6 July Byrd was made an Officer of the French Legion of Honor. At a dinner on 19 July, Byrd and Noville received the Distinguished Flying Cross. Acosta and Balchen were civilians, so they did not receive it.
So by 1927 Byrd had fame, but the question over 1926 was still alive. Could he achieve a success that no one could doubt?

articleEn: In 1928 Byrd began his first Antarctic expedition. This time the aim was not a single flight but to run a complete mission in the vast expanse of ice. The expedition included two ships and three airplanes. Byrd's flagship was the City of New York, and the other ship was the Eleanor Bolling, named after Byrd's mother. The City of New York was actually a Norwegian sealing ship, formerly called the Samson. Some people said it had been near the Titanic when that ship sank, so the vessel already had a famous story of its own.

Their destination was the Ross Ice Shelf, where the expedition's base was to be built. There was nothing but ice for as far as one could see. The base built there was called Little America. The camp was set up on the ice and became home for the months ahead.

Three airplanes went along. The first was a Ford Trimotor named the Floyd Bennett, in memory of the pilot who had recently died, and it was flown by Dean Smith. The second was a Fairchild FC-2W2, the Stars And Stripes, and the third was a Fokker Super Universal monoplane named Virginia, after Byrd's home state. The Stars And Stripes is still preserved today, though sources differ on where it is displayed.

Once the base was established on the Ross Ice Shelf, the work began. Scientific expeditions set out by snowshoe, dog sled, snowmobile and airplane. Byrd supported the use of ski-equipped airplanes, but they came with many operational, logistical and maintenance problems, so large onshore bases were necessary. The expedition also included a 19-year-old American Boy Scout, Paul Allman Siple. The aim was to raise young people's interest in arctic exploration. Siple went on to earn a doctorate, and he may be the only person besides Byrd to take part in all five of Byrd's Antarctic expeditions.

During the first summer there were photographic expeditions and geological surveys. Most importantly, radio contact with the outside world was kept up continuously. Byrd also built ties with powerful people, including Henry Ford, Edsel Ford, John D. Rockefeller Jr. and Vincent Astor. The friendship and admiration of Henry and Edsel Ford played an important part in the Ford Motor Company's sponsorship, and it was a very big support for Byrd. As thanks, Byrd named many Antarctic features after his supporters. The region named for his wife, Marie, is Marie Byrd Land.

So Little America was more than a camp. It was a whole system of science, radio and funding. But the real test was still ahead: the flight to the South Pole. For that he needed a pilot who understood ice and danger. Who was that man? In the next part we hear his story.

articleEn: Now we meet the man who became chief pilot of this flight. Bernt Balchen was a Norwegian pilot who later became an American citizen. He was born on 23 October 1899 at Myren farm in Tveit, near Kristiansand, Norway. His father was a country doctor. He joined the French Foreign Legion and his unit was sent to the Verdun front, but in 1918, before seeing combat, he was called back to Norway. Then, under an assumed name, he took part in the Finnish Civil War with the White Guards as a cavalryman. In one charge his horse was killed. He was badly wounded and took a long time to recover.

He then trained hard in boxing to represent Norway at the 1920 Olympics. He was a boxing champion, a good marksman and an expert skier. His knowledge of survival in snowy regions would later serve him well. While waiting for the Olympics he was also found qualified for flight training, and in 1921 he became a pilot in the Royal Norwegian Navy Air Service. In 1925 he joined the Amundsen-Ellsworth Relief Expedition, sent to Spitsbergen to search for the missing explorer Roald Amundsen. Amundsen became his lifelong friend. In 1926, at Amundsen's urging, Balchen helped prepare the Josephine Ford. Damaged skis were reinforced with wood from lifeboat oars.

Then came the transatlantic flight of 1927. According to sources, Balchen did most of the flying in bad weather, and in the end the plane came down near the French coast. In April 1928, three crew members of the Bremen were stranded on Greenly Island in Canada. Balchen and Floyd Bennett set out to help in a Ford Trimotor. Bennett had earlier developed pneumonia after a crash, and he died on 25 April 1928. One source says this happened during the flight. Balchen flew the remaining eight hours. He was paid 10,000 dollars for the job, but he gave the entire sum to Bennett's widow.

The Ford 4-AT Trimotor modified for the South Pole was named the Floyd Bennett, and Balchen was its chief pilot. Harold June was co-pilot and radio operator. Keeping radio contact going for the whole flight was very important. Ashley McKinley was the flight's photographer, and Byrd was aboard as navigator and expedition leader.

So the crew was four men: Balchen, June, McKinley and Byrd. Their experience was varied, but now all of them had to face one difficulty in a single plane. Balchen later received the Congressional Gold Medal in 1930. But at that moment the question was whether these four men could climb high enough above the ice.

articleEn: On 28 November 1929 a journey was about to begin at Little America that had never been made before: a flight to the South Pole and back. After the first winter the expedition's work had started again. Now Byrd faced his biggest test, the first flight to the South Pole. For Byrd this was not just exploration. Doubts about the 1926 North Pole flight had already been raised, and now the first flight to the South Pole lay before him.

The aircraft was the modified Ford 4-AT Trimotor, named the Floyd Bennett, with three engines. The crew was four: Balchen as chief pilot, June as co-pilot and radio operator, McKinley as photographer, and Byrd as navigator and expedition leader. According to the Navy Cross citation, Byrd took off from Little America in the Floyd Bennett on 28 November.

The way ahead was not just a plain of ice. To reach the South Pole they had to cross territory where the land rises thousands of feet. According to the citation, the ranges and plateaus there were nine to ten thousand feet high, and if a forced landing had occurred, rescue would not have been possible. On this flight the plane's weight and altitude were going to be the biggest problem. The more they carried, the harder it was to climb.

Byrd supported ski-equipped airplanes, even though they had many operational and maintenance problems. Then came a big announcement. On 21 December 1929 Congress, through a special act, made Byrd a rear admiral. Byrd was only 41 years old, which made him the youngest admiral in the history of the United States Navy. For comparison, none of his Annapolis classmates became an admiral until 1942, after 30 years of commissioned service.

Another interesting point: he is one of only four people who became rear admiral directly without holding the rank of captain. The other three include David Dixon Porter, Donald Baxter MacMillan and Frederic R. Harris. MacMillan is the man with whom Byrd went to Greenland in 1925.

The expedition returned to North America on 18 June 1930. This time the outcome was different from 1926, because the American Geographical Society honored it with a gold medal. The film made on the trip, With Byrd at the South Pole, came out in 1930 and showed Byrd's journey to the South Pole. The Navy Cross citation called the flight extraordinary heroism, and this honor became the official recognition of the flight for Byrd. Balchen also received the Congressional Gold Medal in 1930, for his pioneering work in aviation. Byrd had three ticker-tape parades in New York City, in 1926, 1927 and 1930. According to the sources, no one else received such an honor.

Now turn back to 1926. The North Pole flight brought the Medal of Honor, but it also brought doubt. Another honor was the Hubbard Medal, which the National Geographic Society gave him for the North Pole flight, and he was its seventh recipient. Balchen expressed doubt about that flight in 1958. But Floyd Bennett, before his death, had confirmed Byrd's account. In 1996 Byrd's diary came to light. Dennis Rawlins concluded that Byrd flew about 80 percent of the distance. A defender disagrees.

Our sources do not mention such doubts about the South Pole flight. On the contrary, the expedition received a gold medal and official honors. articleEn: Byrd's story did not end there. In the second expedition of 1933-34 he stayed alone at Advance Base for five months and narrowly survived carbon monoxide poisoning. Then in 1946-47 came Operation Highjump, the largest Antarctic expedition up to that time, involving more than 4,000 people. Deep Freeze I of 1955-56 set up permanent bases at McMurdo Sound, Bay of Whales and the South Pole. This is where the permanent US presence in Antarctica began.

Byrd died in Boston on 11 March 1957 and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Balchen died in 1973, and his grave is beside Byrd's. In November 1965 Balchen also took part in the world's first circumnavigation flight over both poles, and he was in the cockpit during four circuits over the South Pole.

So what do we learn from this story? Courage and preparation go together, and Byrd made safety the first priority of his expeditions. One question stays open: how thin were the margins? What would have happened if the plane had not climbed? If you liked this story, please like the video and subscribe to the channel. We will meet again in the next story.

shorts.titleEn: The Plane That Wouldn't Climb: Byrd's South Pole Gamble
shorts.text: کیا ایک جہاز کو اڑانے کے لیے اپنی emergency supplies پھینکنی پڑ سکتی ہیں؟ 28 November 1929 کو Antarctica کے اوپر ایک Ford Trimotor آہستہ آہستہ بلند ہونے کی کوشش کر رہا تھا۔ اس جہاز کا نام Floyd Bennett تھا۔ نیچے برف کا میدان تھا، اور سامنے Antarctic Plateau کی بلندی۔ جہاز کو مناسب اونچائی نہیں مل رہی تھی۔ جہاز میں چار آدمی تھے: Richard Byrd، Bernt Balchen، Harold June اور Ashley McKinley۔ Balchen chief pilot تھے اور Byrd navigator۔ پھر crew نے ایک مشکل فیصلہ کیا۔ خالی gas tanks اور emergency supplies جہاز سے باہر پھینک دی گئیں۔ Navy Cross citation کے مطابق یہ پرواز ایسے علاقے میں تھی جہاں forced landing کی صورت میں مدد پہنچنا ممکن نہیں تھا۔ تو کیا جہاز اوپر جا سکا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aik jahaz ko udane ke liye apni emergency supplies phenkni par sakti hain? 28 November 1929 ko Antarctica ke upar aik Ford Trimotor aahista aahista buland hone ki koshish kar raha tha. Is jahaz ka naam Floyd Bennett tha. Neeche baraf ka maidan tha, aur samne Antarctic Plateau ki bulandi. Jahaz ko munasib oonchai nahi mil rahi thi. Jahaz mein chaar aadmi thay: Richard Byrd, Bernt Balchen, Harold June aur Ashley McKinley. Balchen chief pilot thay aur Byrd navigator. Phir crew ne aik mushkil faisla kiya. Khali gas tanks aur emergency supplies jahaz se bahar phenk di gayeen. Navy Cross citation ke mutabiq yeh parwaz aise ilaqay mein thi jahan forced landing ki soorat mein madad pohanchna mumkin nahi tha. To kya jahaz upar ja saka? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

On 28 November 1929 a Ford Trimotor struggled to climb over the Antarctic Plateau on the first flight to the South Pole.
The crew made a hard choice to lighten the plane.

shorts.titleEn: Did Byrd Really Reach the North Pole in 1926?
shorts.text: کیا ایک مشہور explorer کا سب سے بڑا دعویٰ آج بھی شک کے گھیرے میں ہے؟ 9 May 1926 کو Richard Byrd اور Floyd Bennett نے Fokker tri-motor جہاز Josephine Ford میں North Pole کی طرف پرواز کی۔ پرواز Spitsbergen سے شروع ہوئی اور وہیں واپس آئی، کل 15 گھنٹے 57 منٹ میں۔ دونوں نے دعویٰ کیا کہ وہ North Pole تک پہنچ گئے۔ واپسی پر Byrd قومی hero بنے اور New York میں parade ہوئی۔ 21 December 1926 کو Congress نے دونوں کو Medal of Honor دیا۔ مگر 1926 سے ہی شکوک اٹھتے رہے۔ 1958 میں Bernt Balchen نے جہاز کی رفتار کی بنیاد پر سوال اٹھایا۔ دوسری طرف Bennett کی تحریریں اور interviews Byrd کے بیان کی تصدیق کرتی ہیں۔ تو سچ کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aik mashhoor explorer ka sab se bara dawa aaj bhi shak ke ghere mein hai? 9 May 1926 ko Richard Byrd aur Floyd Bennett ne Fokker tri-motor jahaz Josephine Ford mein North Pole ki taraf parwaz ki. Parwaz Spitsbergen se shuru hui aur wahin wapas aayi, kul 15 ghantay 57 minute mein. Dono ne dawa kiya ke woh North Pole tak pahunch gaye. Wapsi par Byrd qaumi hero bane aur New York mein parade hui. 21 December 1926 ko Congress ne dono ko Medal of Honor diya. Magar 1926 se hi shukook uthte rahe. 1958 mein Bernt Balchen ne jahaz ki raftaar ki bunyad par sawal uthaya. Doosri taraf Bennett ki tehreerein aur interviews Byrd ke bayan ki tasdeeq karti hain. To sach kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
In May 1926 Byrd and Floyd Bennett claimed to have flown over the North Pole, but doubts began almost at once.
Sources disagree, and the debate continues.

shorts.titleEn: 5 Months Alone in Antarctica: Byrd's Advance Base
shorts.text: پانچ مہینے، اکیلے، برف کے بیچ ایک چھوٹے سے station میں! 1933-34 کی دوسری Antarctic expedition میں Richard Byrd نے Advance Base نام کا meteorological station اکیلے چلایا۔ وہاں سے وہ بال بال بچے، کیونکہ ایک poorly ventilated stove سے carbon monoxide کا مسئلہ پیدا ہوا۔ پھر Byrd کی عجیب radio transmissions سے base camp کے لوگ پریشان ہونے لگے۔ انہوں نے Advance Base جانے کی کوشش کی۔ پہلی دو trips اندھیرے، برف اور mechanical مسائل کی وجہ سے ناکام ہو گئیں۔ آخرکار Thomas Poulter، E. J. Demas اور Amory Waite وہاں پہنچ گئے۔ 12 October کو ایک airplane نے Byrd اور Poulter کو واپس base camp پہنچایا۔ اس سفر کا حال Byrd نے اپنی کتاب Alone میں لکھا۔ مگر اس تنہائی میں اور کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Paanch mahine, akelay, baraf ke beech aik chhotay se station mein! 1933-34 ki doosri Antarctic expedition mein Richard Byrd ne Advance Base naam ka meteorological station akelay chalaya. Wahan se woh baal baal bache, kyunke aik poorly ventilated stove se carbon monoxide ka masla paida hua. Phir Byrd ki ajeeb radio transmissions se base camp ke log pareshan hone lage. Unhon ne Advance Base jane ki koshish ki. Pehli do trips andhere, baraf aur mechanical masail ki wajah se nakam ho gayeen. Aakhirkar Thomas Poulter, E. J. Demas aur Amory Waite wahan pahunch gaye. 12 October ko aik airplane ne Byrd aur Poulter ko wapas base camp pohanchaya. Is safar ka haal Byrd ne apni kitab Alone mein likha. Magar is tanhai mein aur kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
During the 1933-34 expedition Byrd manned Advance Base alone for five months.
A rescue effort failed twice before reaching him.
